summary: A Network Host Status report covering July 17 to July 28, 1972. The new IMP software was released on Tuesday, July 18.

plainLanguage.summary: This report records host connection tests from July 17 to July 28, 1972. It also notes a release of new IMP software and explains the status codes used in its tables.

subtitle: BBN's ARPANET host status report for July 17 to July 28, 1972.

tldr.problem: Network users needed information about host availability and service status.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested hosts from its Terminal IMP and recorded the outcomes alongside reported status or predictions.
tldr.outcome: The report notes that new IMP software was released on July 18. RFC 370 obsoletes RFC 367 and was updated by RFC 376.

today: RFC 370 is listed as Unknown. It obsoletes RFC 367 and was updated by RFC 376.

sections.title: Reporting Period and Exclusions
sections.content:
The report covers most Network Hosts from July 17 to July 28. New IMP software was released on Tuesday, July 18.

Hosts intended only to use network services are left out of daily testing. These include Terminal IMPs, the Network Control Center computer used to gather statistics, and several other hosts listed in the report. The BBN Terminal IMP at Network Address 158 is a prototype and is often disconnected while its programs are refined.
sections.plainLanguage: The report covers two weeks of host tests and notes when the network's new IMP software was released. Some user-only hosts were not tested as servers.

sections.title: Host Status and Predictions
sections.content:
A table lists the network address, site, computer, status or prediction, and source of that information for each host. Entries include server, user-only, never and soon, as well as expected months of availability. A star marks a host not included in daily testing.

The report also notes that the NMC at address 1 is a research site that asks users to make prior arrangements. The UCLA IBM-360/91 offered NETRJS, which the BBN Terminal IMP could not test directly.
sections.plainLanguage: One table summarizes what each site said about its host. A star shows which hosts were left out of daily testing.

sections.title: Daily Test Results
sections.content:
The test table gives results and Eastern test times for dates from July 17 to July 28. Its codes distinguish an accessible open host, a dead or inaccessible host, a half-open connection, a refusal, a timeout and a full host. A timeout means the host did not finish the Initial Connection Protocol and open a connection within 60 seconds.

A hash mark means the site had said its system might not be available. Since the Terminal IMP could not test NETRJS at the UCLA IBM-360/91, the report assumed that reaching the NETRJS logger meant the service was functioning.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test result has a letter that describes what happened. The legend also identifies a host that answered but had no network ports available.

items.label: Dead
items.desc: Host was dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.

items.label: Full
items.desc: Host opened a connection, reported all ports in use, and closed it.

items.label: Half open
items.desc: Host opened a connection, then closed it or stopped responding.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: Host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: Host did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds.

references.text: RFC 367, the earlier host status report obsoleted by this RFC.
